text:
Write the main text for my sales page. I'm a bookkeeper and I work only with hair and nail salons. I do monthly books, payroll for up to 10 staff, and sales tax filing.

What's true:
- I have 31 salon clients. 2 left last year, both because they sold their salons.
- I charge $199 a month. Until January it was $149, and I raised it for everyone, including existing clients.
- I close each month's books by the 10th of the next month. I missed that date 3 times last year.
- Last tax season, 9 of my clients told me their accountant charged them less because the books came in clean. One said she saved $800.
- I'm one person. I don't answer the phone on Sundays or Mondays.
- The first call is free and takes 20 minutes.

Keep it to about 350 words, with a button at the end to book the call.

Before I write this, I have five questions. A sales page has to deal with what a salon owner will doubt before they book: whether you know salons, whether one person can be relied on, and whether $199 is worth it. Your facts cover some of that already. These would cover the rest:

1. **What do you know about salons that a general bookkeeper doesn't?** For example, booth rent versus commission staff, tips, retail product sales, or time you spent working in a salon. Everyone claims they "specialize," so this is what makes the claim believable.

2. **The 10th-of-the-month deadline.** You hit it 33 times out of 36 last year. How late were the 3 misses, and do you want the page to promise the 10th? If you do, is there anything you'll stand behind if you miss it? I won't invent a guarantee, so this has to come from you.

3. **Being one person.** If you're sick or on vacation, what happens? And how fast do you reply on the days you work, say same day or within 24 hours? A clear answer turns "one person" into a selling point instead of a worry.

4. **The price.** Did any clients leave when you went from $149 to $199 in January? If nobody did, that's a strong line for the page. Also, what are salon owners usually doing before they come to you: doing it themselves, paying their tax accountant, or using another bookkeeper?

5. **The details the page can't go out without.** Your name and business name, and the booking link for the button. And can I quote the client who saved $800, by first name or as "a nail salon owner in [city]"? Or should she stay unnamed?

If you'd rather skip any of these, tell me and I'll write it without that point. I won't fill the gaps with guesses.

1. I managed a hair salon for 6 years before I became a bookkeeper. That's it beyond what I already gave you.

2. I don't know exactly how late the 3 misses were. Yes, promise the 10th. Since January, if I miss the 10th, that month's fee is free.

3. I don't know what happens if I'm sick or on vacation, and I don't know my typical reply time.

4. I don't know if anyone left because of the price change. What owners are doing before they come to me, I don't know either.

5. I'm Carla Benson, and the business is Chair and Ledger. The button goes to my calendar, and calls are Tuesday to Saturday. I don't have the link with me right now. Keep the $800 client unnamed.

# Bookkeeping for hair and nail salons, from someone who managed one

**Monthly books, payroll and sales tax for one flat fee of $199 a month.**

I'm Carla Benson. Before I became a bookkeeper, I managed a hair salon for six years. I know how a salon week goes, and I know the paperwork is usually what gets left until last.

Chair and Ledger works only with hair and nail salons. I have 31 salon clients right now. Last year two left, and both left because they sold their salons.

## What $199 a month covers

- **Monthly books**, closed by the 10th of the following month
- **Payroll** for up to 10 staff
- **Sales tax filing**

You get all three for one price every month.

## Your books by the 10th, or that month is free

I close each month's books by the 10th of the next month. Last year I missed that date three times. So now, if I miss the 10th, you don't pay for that month. You know when your numbers will be ready, and if they're late, I pay for it, not you.

## Clean books cost less at tax time

Last tax season, nine of my clients told me their accountant charged them less because their books came in clean. One of them said she saved $800. That's about four months of my fee.

When your books are a mess, your accountant has to sort them out before they can start on your taxes, and you pay for that time. When your books arrive clean and on time, that cost goes away.

## You'll always work with me

Chair and Ledger is just me. There's no call center, and no new account manager every few months. The person you talk to is the one doing your books, and she has already learned how your salon works.

I work Tuesday to Saturday. Like most of the salons I work with, I don't answer the phone on Sundays or Mondays.

## Start with a free 20-minute call

Tell me about your salon: how many staff you have, how you pay them, and what's been piling up. I'll tell you how I'd handle it. Calls are Tuesday to Saturday, and the first one is free.

**[ Book your free 20-minute call ]**
</final_document>

A few notes on the draft:

- **Button link:** The button doesn't link anywhere yet. Add your calendar link before the page goes live.
- **The three missed deadlines:** I kept them in on purpose, right before the free-month promise. Owners will believe the guarantee more if they see why you made it. If you'd rather not mention the misses, delete that one sentence and the section still works.
- **What I left out:** The page doesn't mention the January price increase. There's nothing about sick days, vacation cover or how fast you reply, since you didn't know those yet. It also doesn't claim every client saves money at tax time, only what the nine told you.
- **"Like most of the salons I work with":** I guessed that your clients are also closed on Sundays or Mondays. If that's not true, cut that phrase.
- **Length:** It's about 370 words. To get closer to 350, drop the second paragraph of "Clean books cost less at tax time."
